beats.narration_en: Why do tires explode on the highway?
Most blowouts start days earlier, with a tire that's just a little low.
Every time it rolls, the soft sidewall bends flat at the bottom, then springs back.
At sixty miles an hour, that happens fifteen times every second.
All that bending turns into heat, deep inside the rubber.
The heat slowly cooks the glue that holds the steel belts together.
Until the tread peels away, and the tire bursts in a split second.
And tires quietly lose about a pound of air every month.
That's where those shreds of rubber on the highway come from.
